questions.prompt: At root, how does Snellman describe a function?
choices: A A process that may return many unrelated outputs for one input.
B A rule/machine that takes a valid input and produces an output.
C Any equation with two equals signs.
D A list of inequalities with no inputs.
questions.explain: He frames functions as take a valid input, do something, give an output.

questions.prompt: What is the domain of a function, in Snellman’s preferred wording?
choices: A Always exactly the y-values on a graph.
B The entire set of valid inputs you are allowed to plug into f.
C Only the coefficient of x.
D The set of all undefined expressions.
questions.explain: Domain = entire set of valid inputs (“things you are allowed to plug into f”).

questions.prompt: For g(x) = 1/x, what does Snellman conclude about the domain?
choices: A All real numbers including 0.
B All nonzero real numbers (x ≠ 0).
C Only positive integers.
D Only x = 0.
questions.explain: Division by zero is invalid, so the domain excludes 0.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x², what does Snellman say about the range?
choices: A All real numbers, positive and negative.
B Outputs from 0 upward; you cannot get a negative by squaring a real.
C Only the single value 1.
D Exactly the same as the domain with no restriction.
questions.explain: Squaring reals cannot produce negatives; range is [0, ∞).

questions.prompt: Which new arithmetic-like operation on functions does Snellman highlight beyond +, −, ×, ÷?
choices: A Factorial of a function.
B Composition (feeding one function’s output into another).
C Matrix transposition of scalars.
D Taking absolute value of the domain only.
questions.explain: He introduces composition as a new operation not present in ordinary number arithmetic.
